title: Magnets and magnetic fields — invisible forces that shape our world
examTip: Know the difference between permanent and induced magnets. Be able to describe field line patterns, with the direction from N to S outside the magnet.
introTips: Magnetic fields are regions of force. They are found around magnets, and also around wires carrying a current.
Iron is magnetically 'soft'. It is easy to magnetise and demagnetise. Steel is 'hard'. It keeps its magnetism.
Earth itself acts like a giant bar magnet. This is why compasses work.
intro: You rely on magnetism when you stick something to a fridge, use a compass or have an MRI scan. Magnetic fields are invisible, but their effects are real and powerful. They are also the base of how electricity generators and electric motors work. Understand magnets first, and the rest of electromagnetism makes sense.

keyPoints.heading: Permanent and induced magnets
keyPoints.content: A permanent magnet is a material that is always magnetic. It does not need to be placed in a field to be magnetic. Permanent magnets are often made of steel, or of alloys containing cobalt, nickel or neodymium. Every permanent magnet has a north pole and a south pole. The basic rule is: unlike poles attract (N attracts S) and like poles repel (N repels N, S repels S). The force between magnets acts without touching. It is a non-contact force that acts through the magnetic field. An induced (temporary) magnet is a magnetic material that becomes magnetised when placed in a magnetic field. Take it out of the field, and it loses its magnetism. Iron is magnetically 'soft'. It is easy to magnetise and easy to demagnetise. That makes it ideal for induced magnets and electromagnet cores. Steel is magnetically 'hard'. It is harder to magnetise, but it keeps its magnetism. That makes it better for permanent magnets. Ferromagnetic materials can be strongly magnetised: iron, steel, cobalt and nickel. All other materials, like aluminium, copper, wood and plastic, are non-magnetic. Magnetic fields do not affect them.
writeBullets: Permanent magnets — always magnetic. Often made of steel, or alloys of cobalt, nickel or neodymium
Unlike poles attract and like poles repel. It is a non-contact force acting through the field
Induced magnet — magnetised by a field. It loses its magnetism when removed
Iron is 'soft' (easy to magnetise and demagnetise). Steel is 'hard' (keeps its magnetism)
Ferromagnetic materials — iron, steel, cobalt, nickel. Strongly affected by fields
Non-magnetic — aluminium, copper, wood, plastic. Not affected by magnetic fields

keyTerms.def: A material that is always magnetic without needing an external field
A magnetic material that becomes temporarily magnetised inside a magnetic field
Materials that can be strongly magnetised: iron, steel, cobalt, nickel
Easy to magnetise and demagnetise — iron is the classic example

keyPoints.memTip: Iron is SOFT: easy in, easy out. Steel is HARD: once it's in, it stays.
keyPoints.tutor_note: 'Magnetic' and 'ferromagnetic' are often mixed up. Only iron, cobalt, nickel and steel are ferromagnetic. Aluminium is often wrongly thought to be magnetic, because it is shiny and metal-coloured.

keyPoints.heading: Magnetic field lines
keyPoints.content: A magnetic field is a region of space where a force acts on a magnetic material. It also acts on a wire carrying a current. We show magnetic fields using field lines, also called flux lines. A field line shows the direction a free north pole would move. So outside the magnet, field lines go from north to south. Inside the magnet, they go from south to north. Field lines always form unbroken closed loops. Key rules for field lines: - Field lines never cross. If they did, that point would have two field directions, which is impossible. - Where field lines are closer together, the field is stronger. Where they spread apart, the field is weaker. The field is strongest near the poles. - Arrows on field lines always point from N to S (outside the magnet). To plot field lines, use a small plotting compass. Place it near the magnet. The compass needle lines up with the local field direction. Move the compass along, marking each position, to trace out the field lines. Earth's magnetic field: Earth acts like a giant bar magnet. Its field lines come out near the geographic South Pole and go in near the geographic North Pole. So Earth's magnetic south pole is near its geographic north pole. A compass needle's north pole is attracted to Earth's magnetic south. So compass needles point toward geographic north. People have used this for navigation for thousands of years.
writeBullets: Magnetic field — a region where a force acts on a magnetic material
Field lines run from N to S outside the magnet (and S to N inside)
Closer field lines = a stronger field. Further apart = a weaker field
Field lines never cross each other
Plot field lines using a small compass. The needle lines up with the local field
Earth's magnetic south pole is near its geographic north pole. That is why compasses point north

keyTerms.def: A region where a force acts on a magnetic material or current-carrying wire
Lines showing the direction and strength of a magnetic field; run N to S outside the magnet
A measure of the strength of a magnetic field — stronger where field lines are closer

keyPoints.memTip: Field lines: never cross, north to south (outside), closer = stronger.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Field lines that cross are always wrong. Also be clear on Earth's poles. Earth's geographic north = Earth's magnetic south. That is why a compass north pole is attracted to it.

keyPoints.heading: Electromagnetism — magnetic fields from currents
keyPoints.content: In 1820, Hans Ørsted discovered that a current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field around it. This was a huge step. It linked electricity and magnetism for the first time. The field around a straight wire forms concentric circles around the wire. Its direction follows the right-hand grip rule. Wrap your right hand around the wire, with your thumb pointing the way the conventional current flows (from + to −). Your fingers curl in the direction of the magnetic field. Reverse the current → the field reverses direction. What affects the strength of the field around a wire: - Current: more current → a stronger magnetic field - Distance from the wire: further away → a weaker field A solenoid is a coil of wire. When current flows through it, the field inside is uniform and strong. The overall field pattern is the same as a bar magnet's. There is a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other. The right-hand grip rule still applies. Grip the solenoid with your right hand, fingers curling the way the current flows round the coil. Your thumb points to the north pole. A soft iron core inside the solenoid makes the magnetic field much stronger, because iron concentrates the field lines. This is the basis of an electromagnet.
writeBullets: A current-carrying wire produces a circular magnetic field around it
Right-hand grip rule — thumb = current direction, fingers = field direction
More current, or closer to the wire → a stronger field
A solenoid (coil of wire) produces a field like a bar magnet, with N and S poles
An iron core inside a solenoid makes the field much stronger
Reversing the current reverses the field direction

keyTerms.def: A coil of wire that produces a bar-magnet-like field when current flows through it
Thumb points in direction of current; fingers curl in direction of the magnetic field
A solenoid with an iron core — produces a strong magnetic field that can be switched on and off

keyPoints.memTip: Solenoid = bar magnet shape. Add an iron core = electromagnet.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Be able to use the right-hand grip rule in two cases. For a straight wire, your fingers curl around the wire. For a solenoid, your fingers curl the way the current flows round the coil. Your thumb points to the N pole.

keyPoints.heading: Electromagnets and their uses
keyPoints.content: An electromagnet is a solenoid with a soft iron core. It is far stronger than a solenoid without a core, because the iron concentrates and strengthens the magnetic field. Most importantly, it can be switched on and off by controlling the current. This makes it hugely useful compared with permanent magnets. What affects the strength of an electromagnet: - Number of coil turns: more turns → a stronger field - Current: a larger current → a stronger field - Iron core: much stronger than a solenoid with an air core Key uses of electromagnets: - Electric bells: a current switches on the electromagnet → it attracts the iron striker → the striker hits the bell. This breaks the circuit → the electromagnet turns off → a spring returns the striker. The circuit closes again, and it repeats. - Relays: switches controlled electrically. A small current in a control circuit switches on an electromagnet. This closes a switch in a separate high-current circuit. They are used where switching large currents by hand is dangerous. - Circuit breakers: a fault current creates a large magnetic force. This trips a lever and breaks the circuit. Unlike fuses, they can be reset. - Loudspeakers: a permanent magnet and an electromagnet (the voice coil) push on each other. This moves a cone back and forth, making sound waves. - MRI scanners: extremely powerful superconducting electromagnets are cooled to near absolute zero. They make fields strong enough to line up hydrogen atoms in the body. - Scrapyard cranes: large electromagnets lift and drop steel and iron scrap. Permanent magnets could not do this.
writeBullets: Electromagnet = a solenoid with a soft iron core. It can be switched, and is much stronger than an air core
Made stronger by: more turns, a larger current, an iron core
Relays — a small current safely switches a circuit with a large current
Circuit breakers — a fault current trips a magnetic lever, breaking the circuit
Loudspeakers — a voice coil and a permanent magnet push on each other to vibrate a cone
MRI scanners — superconducting electromagnets line up hydrogen atoms in the body

keyTerms.def: A solenoid with an iron core — switchable magnetic field controlled by current
A switch controlled by an electromagnet — small current controls a large current circuit
Zero electrical resistance at very low temperatures — used for very powerful electromagnets in MRI

keyPoints.memTip: Electromagnets: switch it on, switch it off. More turns + more current + an iron core = stronger.
keyPoints.tutor_note: It is easy to forget that relays have a safety purpose. The control circuit and the high-current circuit are kept electrically separate. This matters in exam questions about car starter motors and similar uses.

0.question: A student puts a steel paperclip near a bar magnet, and the paperclip is attracted. When it is taken out of the field, it stays slightly magnetic. Which statement best explains this?
options: Steel is magnetically hard. It keeps its magnetism after being taken out of a field
Steel is magnetically soft. It loses its magnetism easily when taken out of a field
The paperclip became a permanent magnet, because steel cannot be demagnetised
The paperclip was already magnetic before it was put near the bar magnet
0.correctFeedback: Correct. Steel is magnetically hard. It is harder to magnetise than iron, but once magnetised it keeps its magnetism. This is why steel is used for permanent magnets.
0.wrongFeedback: Think about what 'magnetically hard' and 'magnetically soft' mean. Iron is soft: easy to magnetise and easy to demagnetise. Steel is hard: it holds on to its magnetism.

2.question: A wire carrying a current is wound into a solenoid. The number of turns is doubled and the current is halved. What happens to the magnetic field strength?
options: The field strength stays roughly the same
2.correctFeedback: Correct. Doubling the turns doubles the field, and halving the current halves it. These two changes cancel out. So the overall field strength stays roughly the same.
2.wrongFeedback: Both the turns and the current affect field strength. Doubling the turns doubles the field. Halving the current halves it. Work out the net effect: 2 × 0.5 = 1. That is back to the original strength.

3.question: What is the best reason for using an electromagnet instead of a permanent magnet in a scrapyard crane?
options: The electromagnet can be switched off to release the metal scrap
The electromagnet is cheaper to make than a permanent magnet
The electromagnet makes a stronger field in all directions
Permanent magnets do not attract iron and steel
3.correctFeedback: Exactly right. The key advantage is that you can switch off the electromagnet by cutting the current. This drops the metal scrap exactly where it is needed. A permanent magnet could not do this.
3.wrongFeedback: Think about what makes electromagnets so useful compared with permanent magnets. The clue is what happens when you switch off the current.

commonMistakes: Drawing field lines that cross each other. Field lines can never cross. Each point in a field has only one direction.
Thinking aluminium is magnetic because it is a shiny metal. Only ferromagnetic materials (iron, steel, cobalt, nickel) are attracted to magnets.
Mixing up magnetically soft and hard. Iron is SOFT (easy to magnetise and demagnetise). Steel is HARD (keeps its magnetism). Soft iron is used for cores, and steel for permanent magnets.
Saying field lines go from S to N outside the magnet. Outside the magnet, field lines always go from N to S. That is the direction a north pole would move.
examTips: When describing a magnetic field, always give the direction of the field lines (N to S outside). Also say that closer lines mean a stronger field.
For electromagnet questions, three factors increase the strength: more turns, a larger current and an iron core. Mention all three if asked.
The right-hand grip rule: thumb = the direction of conventional current. Your fingers curl in the direction of the magnetic field around the wire.

Induced magnet — magnetised by a field. It loses its magnetism when removed
Iron = magnetically soft (easy to magnetise and demagnetise). Steel = hard (keeps its magnetism)
Ferromagnetic materials: iron, steel, cobalt, nickel only
Magnetic field lines: N to S outside the magnet. They never cross. Closer = a stronger field
Right-hand grip rule: thumb = current direction. Fingers = field direction around the wire
Solenoid = a coil of wire. Its field is like a bar magnet's, with N and S poles

Relay: a small current controls a large current. An electromagnet closes a switch
Earth's geographic north = Earth's magnetic south (compass N pole attracted to it)
